Fierce national pride, identity, honor and sense of superiority before the Second World War; two or three generations of repentance and humiliation after it; and then, as the postwar economic boom put Germany back at the top of the industrial world, the pride and superiority came back. Together these have given Germans a complicated character and a peculiar place in Europe.

“You are so German!”

“I don’t give a shit. I’m not German.”

You hear exchanges like this all the time when Europeans chat.

  1. Arrogance. It’s bone-deep, and it pops out from every angle now and then.
  2. Fussiness (the earthier Chinese word for it is ruder still). Every last detail has its rules and regulations. A colleague of mine, after two days of wrangling with Sparkasse, his savings bank, to enable foreign payments on his card, confessed: “Sometimes feel shamed to be a German.”
  3. Persecution complex. Brainwashed by Datenschutz (data protection). There are hardly any surveillance cameras in the whole country, so when there’s a crime or a traffic accident, people are often left groping in the dark. One colleague resolutely deleted WhatsApp after Facebook bought it, saying it no longer felt safe; needless to say, he’s not on Facebook. Who the fxxk gives a shit about you.... When it comes to Datenschutz, every German thinks they’re Angela Merkel.
  4. Compulsive German teachers. German is the most beautiful and most useful language on earth, and every German is personally devoted to teaching it free of charge. A while ago I was riding in a car in Spain with a Spaniard, a Swede, a Norwegian and a German, with Spanish radio playing. Then the German said: “I found Spanish is such a harsh language.” Dead silence fell over the whole car...
  5. Clannishness, oblivious to their surroundings. No matter how many people around them can’t understand or speak German, as soon as >2 Germans get together they’re off, chatting and laughing away in German, and everyone else might as well be invisible.
